title: DeepRefine: Agent-Compiled Knowledge Refinement via Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: DeepRefine: Agent-Compiled Knowledge Refinement via Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Agent-compiled knowledge bases provide persistent external knowledge for large language model (LLM) agents in open-ended, knowledge-intensive downstream tasks. Yet their quality is systematically limited by incompleteness , incorrectness , and redundancy , manifested as missing evidence or cross-document links, low-confidence or imprecise claims, and ambiguous or coreference resolution issues. Such defects compound under iterative use, degrading retrieval fidelity and downstream task performance. We present DeepRefine , a general LLM-based reasoning model for agent-compiled knowledge refinement that improves the quality of any pre-constructed knowledge bases with user queries to make it more suitable for the downstream tasks. DeepRefine performs multi-turn interactions with the knowledge base and conducts abductive diagnosis over interaction history, localizes likely defects, and executes targeted refinement actions for incremental knowledge base updates. To optimize refinement policies of DeepRefine without gold references, we introduce a Gain-Beyond-Draft (GBD) reward and train the reasoning process end-to-end via reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent downstream gains over strong baselines.

Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent downstream gains over strong baselines. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in handling natural language understanding and generation tasks ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Jaech et al., 2024 ) . And retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds LLMs in external knowledge bases outside model parameters ( Lewis et al., 2020 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) . A dominant recipe indexes external knowledge as vectors for dense retrieval. Graph-based RAG systems additionally organize salient content into graph-structured knowledge bases to support multi-hop retrieval and reasoning ( Edge et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2024 ; Gutiérrez et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . In both cases, the external knowledge base is usually built once and static at serving time, which provides LLMs with richer external knowledge and enhances their capabilities in domain-specific or knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet a static knowledge base is largely stateless with respect to ongoing use. It does not accumulate structured lessons from repeated queries, user-specific context, or iterative agent workflows. Recent agent-compiled knowledge bases (e.g., LLM-Wiki ( Karpathy, 2026 ) ) address this gap by having LLM-based agents ingest sources, synthesize articles, and maintain cross-references over time. For example, toolkits that compile documents using agentic workflows and file outputs back into a user-owned persistent store. As shown in the left part of Figure 1 , such systems make external knowledge bases evolvable rather than frozen at test time. Figure 1 : The quality problems of agent-compiled knowledge bases (left) and the challenges of knowledge base refinement (right). Despite this progress, agent-compiled knowledge bases often exhibit systematic quality defects, including incompleteness , incorrectness , and redundancy ( Subagdja et al., 2024 ; Cimiano and Paulheim, 2017 ) . In practice, these defects manifest as missing evidence chains or cross-document links, low-confidence or imprecise assertions, and ambiguous or coreference resolution issues. Such issues compound and degrade both retrieval fidelity and end-task performance. Recent studies mainly optimize the construction policy of knowledge base builders ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Tsang et al., 2025 ) , however, in many real deployments the knowledge base has already been constructed, so re-training the constructor and re-compiling the whole knowledge base is often expensive and operationally impractical at scale ( Choubey et al., 2024 ; Wolff and Bennati, 2026 ) , motivating a post-construction agent-compiled knowledge refinement paradigm. Achieving effective agent-compiled knowledge refinement presents two core challenges: (1) defect localization , i.e., identifying problematic regions in a large knowledge base without performing expensive traversal checks; and (2) policy optimization without golden references , i.e., learning effective refinement strategies when no reference refinement actions or golden knowledge bases are available. As shown in the right part of Figure 1 , Challenge (1) arises because compiled knowledge bases are typically large and relationally connected, making exhaustive inspection infeasible for locating defects that stem from incompleteness, incorrectness, or redundancy ( Dong et al., 2025 ) . Challenge (2) arises because the LLM-based agents have difficulty refining knowledge bases and learning how to refine knowledge bases. The real-world refinement lacks golden references. We generally do not observe the “correct” sequence of refinement actions that best aligns a knowledge base with downstream tasks. Consequently, learning effective policies requires training objectives that can evaluate refinement quality through downstream task utility signals. To address these challenges, we propose DeepRefine , a general LLM-based reasoning model for agent-compiled knowledge refinement that improves any pre-constructed knowledge base with user queries to make it more suitable for the downstream tasks. DeepRefine follows a three-step reasoning process: Answerability Judgement Loop , Error Abduction , and Refinement Actions Generation . For Challenge (1), instead of traversing the full knowledge base, DeepRefine performs multi-turn query-conditioned interaction with external knowledge to localize potentially defective neighborhoods, substantially reducing refinement complexity while preserving effectiveness. For Challenge (2), DeepRefine abductively infers likely defect causes from interaction histories, then generates refinement actions to update the knowledge base incrementally. Because the utility of refinement actions is only observable through downstream task performance and is non-differentiable, we introduce a Gain-Beyond-Draft (GBD) reward and optimize the refinement policy end-to-end via reinforcement learning. In summary, we make the following main contributions: • To the best of our knowledge, DeepRefine is the first general LLM-based reasoning model for agent-compiled knowledge refinement , capable of refining any pre-constructed knowledge base using only user queries to make it more suitable for the downstream tasks. • We design a three-step reasoning process including Answerability Judgement Loop , Error Abduction , and Refinement Actions Generation . We further introduce a Gain-Beyond-Draft (GBD) reward with reinforcement learning to enhance the knowledge base refinement capabilities of LLMs. • We conduct extensive experiments across five datasets to demonstrate that DeepRefine can steadily improve the performance of state-of-the-art baseline methods. 2 Related Work 2.1 Agent-Compiled Knowledge Base Management Agent-compiled knowledge bases are effective because they usually capture relational and multi-hop dependencies, organize evidence hierarchically ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and support efficient retrieval ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Different from graph-enhanced RAG methods that largely treat constructed structures as static artifacts ( Edge et al., 2024 ; Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024 ) , recent agent memory systems (e.g., Zep ( Rasmussen et al., 2025 ) , Mem0 ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) ) emphasize continuous maintenance and evolution. Existing RL-based approaches, such as Mem- α \alpha ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , Memory-R1 ( Yan et al., 2025 ) , and AutoGraph-R1 ( Tsang et al., 2025 ) , primarily optimize construction-time knowledge base management policies. In contrast, our work focuses on post-construction refinement of already deployed agent-compiled knowledge bases. 2.2 LLMs and Reinforcement Learning Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ) is an effective optimization framework for improving the sequential decision-making capabilities of LLMs through learning from environmental interaction and reward feedback ( Xi et al., 2025 ) . Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) is one of the foundational methods used to align LLM outputs with preferences. And Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) have provided scalable and efficient optimization algorithms for various structured decision-making tasks in several domains. For example, Graph-R1 ( Luo et al., 2025 ) employs RL to learn effective graph-structured tools navigation to retrieve more accurately. Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) trains LLMs to optimize web search queries using RL to maximize final answer correctness and s3 ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) further proposes a principled, model-agnostic reward signal that quantifies improvements over standard retrieval. 2.3 Knowledge Refinement Knowledge refinement aims to mitigate incompleteness , incorrectness , and redundancy in existing artifacts ( Subagdja et al., 2024 ; Cimiano and Paulheim, 2017 ) . Classical knowledge graph (KG) completion is one of the knowledge refinement methods, such as KG-BERT ( Yao et al., 2019 ) and KGRefiner ( Saeedizade et al., 2022 ) , are typically limited to adding links or relations. Entity alignment and disambiguation methods, such as NeuSymEA ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and K-NED ( Feng et al., 2020 ) , focus on correction and simplification. In contrast, knowledge refinement has a broader scope that subsumes both types of operations ( Cimiano and Paulheim, 2017 ) , yet remains underexplored. TRAIL ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) enables LLM-based agents to iteratively explore and update KGs during reasoning, however, its edits are not explicitly optimized against downstream task utility. Our method instead learns refinement policies with an explicit downstream reward, yielding tighter alignment between knowledge base updates and end-task performance. 3 Preliminaries In this section, we formalize the knowledge base and the refinement task with respect to RAG-based downstream tasks. We represent a knowledge base as structured triples that are more general and not limited to classical KG triples. The heads and tails may be entities, events, or document-grounded spans, which we term as knowledge items, and relations may capture taxonomy, time, causality, or cross-document linkage. We denote the pre-constructed knowledge base by a set of triples 𝒢 f = { ( h , r , t ) ∣ h , t ∈ ℰ f , r ∈ ℛ f } \mathcal{G}_{\text{f}}=\{(h,r,t)\mid h,t\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{f}},\,r\in\mathcal{R}_{\text{f}}\} , where ℰ f \mathcal{E}_{\text{f}} is the set of knowledge items and ℛ f \mathcal{R}_{\text{f}} is the set of relations. The knowledge base may be produced by any LLM-based constructors. We are given a set of user queries 𝒬 = { q 1 , q 2 , … , q N } \mathcal{Q}=\{q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{N}\} related to the 𝒢 f \mathcal{G}_{\text{f}} . The goal of agent-compiled knowledge base refinement is to update 𝒢 f \mathcal{G}_{\text{f}} with user queries in 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} to make it more suitable for the downstream RAG tasks.
